title: The Chain That Names the Dead

intro.text: You are the last heir of a struck-out house. You have kept the dead title in a cold vault while the city below rewrote itself in steam and iron. The last steward pressed your black signet into your hand as the archive door closed. The new engine city sealed your name from the registry before you could leave the upper levels.

description.text: {C02}'s conviction sits on you like soot. Your mouth tastes the engine's oath. The black signet is warm as a live coal in your fist.
{C02}'s doubt has left you hollow. The signet is a cold ring of iron in your fist. Your face looks like a name erased in rain.
{C01}'s loyalty has soaked into you. Your sleeves are wet from the lock. Your throat carries the old house's cadence.
{C01}'s loyalty has turned to fear in you. Your knuckles are bruised from the trench. The black signet looks too large for your palm.
{C03}'s memory has opened in you. The steam between levels has a name in your mouth. Your ribs ache with a drowned archive.
{C03}'s memory has closed over you. You smell of brackish water. The names you were not allowed to speak sit in your throat like stones.
Your hands are rope-burned. Your ears ring with the lower gears. The air in your lungs moves a half-second late. The title you carried has left a red seam across your palms.
You are a struck-out name in a wet coat. The black signet is cold in your fist. The city below has already forgotten the shape of your face.

says.text: After the lower gears, the house in you is no longer a room. It is a seam in the air. You are not sure whether you are the heir or the thing being opened.
The last steward pressed the black signet into your hand while the archive door closed. You have been carrying a house the size of a coffin through a city that has stopped believing in houses.
{C02}'s conviction has made {C02} a man who has already buried the city's fall. You are not sure if you hate {C02} for it or envy the weight {C02} carries.
{C02}'s conviction is cracking. You can see the city's fall in {C02}'s eyes before {C02} says it. You wonder if {C02} took your seat to spare you the knowing.
{C02} took your title's seat and wears the engine like a suit of armor. When {C02} speaks of the core, your black signet feels like a key to the wrong door.
{C01} kept your name when the registry was rewritten. Now {C01}'s loyalty is a wet rope around your ribs. You do not know if {C01} is holding you up or holding you down.
{C01}'s loyalty has a bruise in it. {C01} looks at the brass key as if it might open a mouth. You are afraid {C01} has kept your name because {C01} is afraid of the red seam it leaves on your palms.
{C01} carries the brass key to the steam doors and calls you by a name the new city has no use for. You do not know if that is comfort or a leash.
{C03}'s memory has a voice in the steam. When it recites the names you are not allowed to speak, your own name comes out clean. You do not know if you are hearing the old order or drowning in it.
{C03}'s memory has gone quiet under the waterline. The names you are not allowed to speak sit in your throat. You are not sure whether you are keeping them or becoming them.
{C03} recites the old names in the steam between levels. Every time you hear them, your black signet feels heavier, as if the dead are checking whether you can still carry them.
Deeper down, the need has stopped sounding like proof. It sounds like a name being fed to a gear. You are afraid the answer will be that you were always the chain.
You need to know if the title is still a house or only a chain. The engine wants it to be a chain. The archive wants it to be a house. Your hands are not sure which one they are gripping.
At the end of the chain, the question no longer asks which name will save you. It asks which name will be allowed to keep you. The silence under the engine is not an answer.

Whether you reclaim the title as a house or let it become a chain that names the dead instead of the living. The old order pulls you toward a name that can be spoken. The engine pulls you toward a name that can keep turning. Neither promise is safe.

jocelin_loyalty.meaning: How far Jocelin believes the old name can still be carried as a house rather than a chain that must grind him out.

aylmer_conviction.meaning: How far Aylmer believes the engine must be fed with old names to keep the city from falling.

matilda_memory.meaning: How far Matilda believes the old names can still be spoken aloud before the steam swallows them.

description.text: You stand in a circular ballroom hung over a steam chasm, its floor a sheet of smoked glass, its rim ringed by iron steam vents. A riveted archive door stands in the nearest wall. Iron chandeliers with green gas lamps swing above the dance floor. The air carries wet wool, oil, and the chasm's hot mineral breath. A black ring is worn into the glass where banners have hung for years.

You stand in a middle-level passage under the glass-floored ballroom. The floor runs down toward the engine side, a throat in the stone. Blackened brass rails and a chain of stamped links run along the wall. The air is wet with oil and the smell of hot iron. A cracked lamp throws a yellow circle on a floor marked by old oil stains. The deeper end opens into a landing where the stone stops being level.

You stand on the seam landing where the passage meets the engine gates. The floor is a slope of riveted iron and black stone. The wall is pitted with rivet handholds and a tide channel cut for steam. The air tastes of oil, hot iron, and something older than the city. The far end is a wall of riveted iron, scored with a dark line where the metal was cut. The place is built to be crossed, not to be left behind.

You stand in a wet, oily waiting bay before the engine gates. The black slab floor is scored with a drain channel that will not dry. A wall of iron hooks runs along one side, each ring worn to a bright lip where hands have gripped it. The registry lectern stands under a hood that drips a slow bead of steam. The air tastes of hot iron and salt. Beyond the gate mouth, the core's turn is a sound felt in the teeth.

You stand in a narrow bay of blackened brick where the lower doors meet the steam. The floor is slick with a film that will not dry. The chain rail runs along the wall, its links dark with old oil and older use. A seal plate is set into the door frame, its face worn to a mirror by hands that checked it. The archive mouth breathes cold white steam from a crack in the wall.

The engine gates open onto the gear-throne engine room, a rectangle of black iron. The core's turn presses in the chest. Gate channels run along the floor, filled with oil that will not dry, their edges worn bright by the gate leaves. A black stone ledge runs along the threshold, its edge worn where hands have rested. The air moves in hot, wet waves, smelling of burned metal and something older than metal.

You stand at a black iron pit at the engine room's bottom, where a gear-throne of interlocking wheels rises from the floor like a seat grown out of the machine. Oil slicks the floor; the air smells of hot metal and old rust. Rivets circle the pit; walls are scored with names struck out by generations of clerks. The only light is the machine's dull glow behind the gears' teeth.

You stand in a narrow alcove cut into the engine wall, lined with iron shelves for registries and a stone desk where titles are signed. The air is dry and papery, with a smell of lamp oil and ink. A small lock set into the shelf waits for an engine key, and a channel along the floor carries drips away into the dark. The alcove is lit by a fixed lamp whose glass is clouded with heat.

You face a round iron door set in the wall between the registry alcove and the deeper archive, rimmed by a steam channel hot to the touch. White steam pours through its gaps in a constant low roar, carrying the smell of boiled paper and mineral water. The door has a keyhole, a cold handle, and a burn mark shaped like a hand around its edge. Beyond it, the old archive waits behind a mouth of iron.

You stand on a walkway of grated iron around the gear-throne pit, where the steam crews stand to work the core. The rail is black with soot, and the floor is grated so oil can fall through. Hold bars and hooks are fixed along the wall for bracing against the machine, and a drum of oil hangs from a hook beside the gallery lamp. The gallery opens onto the pit with a view of the throne, the registry alcove, and the steam door.

You face a spiral of black iron and cracked glass descending from the ballroom floor into the steam chasm, each step worn to a lip by generations of aristocratic heels. The handrail is polished to a dull shine, studded with broken buttons, gloves, and one small crown. At the bottom, a seam landing waits under a dripping grate, where the air smells of hot oil and old blood.

You stand in a squat iron chamber, where two doors lean against their frames and never fully close, their edges dripping hot condensate onto the floor while the walls hum with pressure gauges whose needles tremble in directions that do not agree. Under your boots a floor grate groans. Beyond it the engine gates wait like a throat.

exits.label: through the pressure lock to the engine gates

description.text: You stand in a vertical throat of riveted bronze that drops from the core threshold past the lower doors into the gear-throne. Oil slicks the walls, and older light leaves a residue that bends around the seams. The steps appear only when you are not watching, and the count is always one number too many. Below, the great gears turn less like machinery than a heart deciding to stop.
The round iron wheel is set in the rim, its spokes stiff with scale. Turn it, and the chasm below answers with a breath of white steam.
You look down through smoked glass dark enough to hide what lies under it. A hairline flaw runs from one corner of the dance floor to the archive door.
The riveted iron door is set into the ballroom wall. Its lock is a black ring of dead metal. Many hands have worked it until the rivets are bright.
The leather-bound registry is swollen with damp. The first page is loose, and the ink on it has gone the color of dried blood.
A heavy brass key hangs on a chain, its teeth filed shallow. The bow is worn to a smooth oval from too many turns.
A ring of cold black iron. The Wode mark is worn smooth by generations of thumbs. When you look at it, the city's new registry has no place for the name inside.
Old banners hang from a wire rack, their silk rotted to the color of tea. The last one is tied with a cord of black wire, as if it were meant to be dropped, not hung.
Iron chandeliers hold green glass shades, their chains stiff with rust. One shade is cracked, and the lamp inside has been replaced with a smaller one.

The chain of blackened links runs the length of the wall. Each link is stamped with a house name in faded ink. The last link is bent into a spiral, as if it once tried to hold something heavier than a title.
A strip of old banner is stuck to the rail. The cloth is soft and grey with damp. The fringe is braided from wire, not thread, and steam has chewed it.
The brass gauge has a needle that no longer points to level. It points to the direction the passage wants to fall. The glass is fogged over a scratch that says DOWN.
The rail of blackened brass is worn smooth where hands gripped it during the leaning of the city. A ring of white grime marks the height of a man who is no longer here.
The oil stain spreads in the shape of a hand, but with too many fingers. The center is dry and black, like a coin that has been spent.
The brass lamp has a cracked globe. It throws a yellow circle that never quite reaches the chain. The oil in its base is dark. The wick has been trimmed with a knife, not scissors.
The plate of iron is set into the wall for hands. Its edges are rolled to stop a finger from being sheared. One edge is stamped with a number that matches no floor in the city's maps.

The page is torn from the old registry. Steam has blurred its ink. One name is struck through in black ink. The struck line is not a mistake; it is a wound, and the paper around it is stiff with salt.
The door is riveted plate. Its seam is packed with black rubber. Its wheel is cold to the touch. Where the wheel meets the frame, a hairline crack runs in the shape of a broken finger.
The key is black iron, with a head like a gear tooth. It is warm even when it has not been used. The bow is stamped with a number that the engine has not yet learned to read.
The glove is torn at the knuckles. The leather splits along the back of the hand. The fingers are bent inward, as if the hand tried to keep holding something after it was broken.
Rows of rivets are set into the wall for hands. Their heads are worn bright by sweat and oil. One rivet is loose, and it turns when you breathe.
The channel is cut into the floor to carry steam when the corridor leans. Its edges are blackened and slick. The water in it moves against the lean, as if the deeper city has its own weather.
The handprint is in the oil on the plate wall. It has five fingers and a thumb, and the print is still wet. The middle finger is pressed hard enough to crack the oil into a star.
The oil slick covers the landing in a black mirror, broken by the slope into long silver lines. It smells of hot iron. It has not dried since the city learned to lean.
The wheel is black iron, set into the plate wall. Its spokes are worn to a shine by hands that did not want to be sealed in. The rim is notched so a key can be turned by feel, in the dark.

A thick ledger with a blackened cover, its pages swollen at the edges, the last line written in fresh ink that still beads like water. The crews' names are in a hand that presses too hard. The old names are listed under the heading Ballast.

A row of heavy iron hooks set into the wall, their rings polished where hands have gripped them. Each hook is bent slightly outward from force. The lowest one is darker than the rest, as if it has held the most weight.
A slab of iron with a sloped plate, a clamp for ledgers, and a drip lip stained black. The plate is notched from years of quills and keys. The clamp's hinge is polished from use.
A bench of black iron with a notch for a tool. Its seat is worn to a hollow where foremen sat. The edge is bright where hands have wiped oil off it, and the legs are set in a plate of rust.

A flat token of black iron with a notch for a chain, worn smooth where it has been carried in a fist. The foreman's initials are worn almost away. The token is warm with the heat of the hand that holds it.

Two massive iron doors set in the bay. Their edges are ground bright where they pass each other, and the hinges are oiled with a black smear. The faces are scarred by old force, and the tide channel runs along their base like a vein.

A rail of heavy links along the wall. One link is larger than the rest, worn smooth where a chain has been fastened and pulled. The links are dark with old oil, and the rail's end is set in a plate of rust.

A square plate of dark metal in the door frame. Its face is marked with a shallow groove and a nick where a key has been struck. The plate is warm to the touch, and the groove is filled with a film of old oil.

A wheel of blackened iron set into the wall. Its spokes are clogged with scale, and the rim is marked with notches for the tide's height. The wheel is stiff to turn, and the notches are worn smooth by hands that checked it.

A low mouth in the brick, framed with a lip of rusted iron. The archive door's breath comes through as white steam. The lip is scored with names worn almost away, and the steam carries the smell of wet paper and old ink.

Two channels of black iron set into the floor. They are filled with a film of oil that will not dry, their edges worn to a bright lip by the gate leaves. The channels run with a slow current, and the oil smells of hot metal and something older than metal.

A ledge of black stone at the threshold. Its edge is worn to a lip, and a ring of scale is fused into the rock where the core's heat has pressed against it. The stone is warm to the touch, and the lip is bright where hands have rested.

The mouth of the gear-throne engine room is a rectangle of black iron. The gears are a sound felt in the bones, and the rim is scored with old force. The throat breathes hot, wet air, and the gears' turn is a pressure in the chest.

A plate of black iron set into the gear throat. Its edge is sharp with scale, and a crack runs from one corner like a vein. The plate is warm to the touch, and the crack is filled with a film of old oil.

A gauge of black glass set into the core ledge. Its needle is stuck at the last mark, and the face is clouded with steam. The numbers are worn almost away, and the glass is warm to the touch, as if the core's heat has pressed through it.

You see a seat of black iron gears, each tooth worn to a dull mirror, with a hollow in the back where a chain can sit. The center wheel is cold to the eye and warm to the hand. The whole throne turns with a sound like a slow heartbeat.

You see a circular slot in the floor before the throne, its rim polished by chain links passing through it. The well is deep enough to swallow a hand. The chain that turns in it leaves a black groove in the iron.

You see a round gap in the gear wall, rimmed with teeth, dark enough to swallow the light from the throne. When the machine opens it, the dark inside does not look like absence. It looks like a mouth full of turning.

You see a cylinder of brass and iron set into the throne's arm, scored with rows of names that can be struck out one by one. A small peephole shows the drum's edge. The names nearest your hand are already blurred by use.
You see a flat plate of iron beside the name drum, with a single groove for a key and a chip of rust where a name has been struck before. The plate is warm. The groove is worn to a shine.
You see a brass spout fixed above the throne, dripping oil in a steady thread onto the gears below. The drip has worn a pale line in the iron. Oil pools in a dark ring at the base of the throne.

You see a long shelf of black iron bolted to the alcove wall, with notches for registries and a small hook for a signet. The notches are worn smooth where books have been pulled out and replaced. A thin film of dust lies in every groove.
You see a heavy lock set into the shelf, its keyhole shaped for an engine key rather than a household pin. The lock's face is scratched with tally marks. The keyhole is dark with old oil.
You see a column of old paper bundles tied with black cord, their edges stained with water and rust. The top bundle is loose. A single page has slipped out to lie flat on the shelf like a dead leaf.
You see a slab of dark stone set into the desk, its surface worn to a shallow basin where a signet can press. The stone is cool and faintly oily. The basin holds a ring of old ink like a dried tear.
You see a small glass well fixed to the desk, its mouth sealed with a disc of dried ink. A hairline crack runs through the glass. The ink inside has settled into a black mirror.
You see a narrow slot in the shelf where struck pages are dropped into the machine below. The slot's edges are blackened. A faint tremor runs through it when the core turns.
You see a round iron door set in the wall, its rim hot enough to blister bare skin. The door's keyhole is worn to a bright ring. The handle is cold where the iron meets the steam's breath.

You see a slow river of white steam pouring from the door's gaps, carrying the smell of boiled paper and mineral water. The steam moves in long, patient folds. It does not disperse so much as thicken where it meets the air.

You see a mouth of iron behind the steam door, its shelves black with age and its pages swollen with damp. The archive's breath is warm and sour. The names inside it are already half-dissolved into the steam.
You see a cold iron handle fixed to the steam door, its surface worn smooth by many hands. A thin film of condensation runs down its base. The handle's grip is slightly too wide for a fist.

You see a round gauge set into the wall beside the door, its needle trembling at the edge of the red line. The glass is fogged with heat. The casing is pitted with tiny holes where steam has forced its way out.

You see a rail of blackened iron running along the steam door's frame, its surface blistered where steam has flashed against it. The rail is still warm. The burn marks form a pattern that looks almost like a handprint.

You see a row of heavy hooks fixed to the gallery wall, each one forged from a single piece of black iron. The hooks are worn smooth where hands have braced against them. Their points are dark with old oil.
You see a thick iron bar set across the gallery floor, its ends anchored in the grating. The bar is slick with oil. Its surface is marked with the dents of many fists.
You see a small brass bell hanging from a hook beside the gallery lamp, its clapper missing. The bell's surface is dented. A thin layer of soot has settled into its rim.
You see a pair of iron lanterns fixed to the gallery rail, their glass panes clouded with heat. The lanterns burn with a low, blue flame. Their light throws long shadows across the grated floor.

You see a dented drum of black iron hanging from a hook, its spout clogged with congealed oil. The drum's surface is marked with tally cuts. A thin stream of oil runs down its side into a dark stain on the grating.
You see a short iron lever set into the gallery wall, its handle wrapped in a strip of oiled leather. The lever's base is warm. Its mechanism clicks faintly when the core turns.
A silver circlet, split by a gear-tooth, is still warm. It fits a head that is no longer there.
Each pane is etched with the names of former claimants, many scratched out by a nervous hand.
When your eyes are elsewhere, the needles spin, each pointing to a different depth.
Under your boots the grate is a rectangle of bars bent upward, shaped by something that tried to climb up from below.
Count them twice and the number shifts. The extra step is always the one you almost miss.
You read each rivet. Each is stamped with a different date, and every date falls in the same minute.
A page from the old archive. Your name is crossed out in wet ink and resealed with engine wax. The strike-through has begun to lift every time you pass a steam door.
A small brass key that fits the title's cold vault, though the vault is now under the engine's floor. It is warm in your hand, which is wrong.
A short brass hammer wears a steam coil around its handle. It is warm from use, and the rivets in its magazine are still bright.
A dented cup has a chip in the rim. The water inside steams, and the copper has gone black where the heat has touched it.
A heavy chain of blackened links lies cold enough to burn. It has no clasp that opens easily, and the last link is worn smooth by old hands.
You see a rag soaked in gear oil, still stiff with rust.
You see a brass thimble, blackened where it was used to hold a burning page.
You see a wet token from the name stacks, warm and trying to hold a shape.

C01.name: Jocelin Tanner

description.text: {C01} stands with the chain across his wrist and the brass key in his fist, face turned toward the steam, waiting for it to speak his name.
{C01} has his back half to you, the chain dragging at his wrist, the brass key cold and loose in his ruined hand.
{C01}'s hand is broken where the seam bit it; the brass key still sits in the ruined grip, and the chain at the wrist is wet with the steam's answer.
{C01} stands with no name left in the old registry, the brass key warm in his fist, the steam already closing behind him.
{C01} is old and bent by the descent, a servant's coat black with oil, the brass key on a chain at his wrist.

here.text: {C01} has the old registry against his chest and the brass key held out to you.
{C01} has his back to the steam and the chain pulling at his wrist.
{C01} has his broken hand around the brass key and the chain dragging him sideways.
{C01} has the brass key in his hand and the title's chain tight at his wrist.

says.text: 'The key is warm,' {C01} says, holding it out. 'It knows where it is going.'
'You took it without asking,' {C01} says, not looking at you. 'Now it is cold.'
'The key is warm,' {C01} says. 'It will not be given to a stranger.'
'The name is not a crown,' {C01} says, pressing the registry against his chest. 'It is a chain.'
'You wear it like a right,' {C01} says, and the chain at his wrist tightens. 'The house is heavier than you.'
'The house name is a burden,' {C01} says. 'A burden must be carried.'
'One name remains,' {C01} says. 'It is mine to strike.'
'You struck it without me,' {C01} says, and the steam answers for him. 'Now the house has no voice.'
'The last name is mine,' {C01} says, holding the key to the steam. 'Let it be struck.'
'One name remains,' {C01} mutters. 'It will not be spoken carelessly.'
'Hold it with me,' {C01} says, taking the chain in his good hand. 'A servant may choose his death.'
'You pulled me by it,' {C01} says, and does not forgive you. 'Now I am only a link.'
'The chain is not a punishment,' {C01} says. 'It is the house, walking.'
'{C02} calls the steam a release,' {C01} says. 'I have seen what it keeps.'
'{C02} has the engine key,' {C01} says, and his hand closes on his own. 'We are both ballast to him.'
'{C02} serves the machine,' {C01} says. 'I serve the house.'
'{C03} keeps the names in the steam,' {C01} says. 'Let {C03} finish what {C03} began.'
'{C03}'s voice is spent,' {C01} says, and the steam thins. 'The names will go with {C03}'.
'{C03} is colder than the room,' {C01} says. 'But {C03} knows the old ink.'
{C01} wipes his hand on his apron and does not look up. '{C05} keeps the crews breathing by the hour. {C05} will not kneel to a name that cannot pay its steam.'
{C01} traces a black smudge on the rail. 'They made it to look like the world above, so the lords could forget the depth. When the glass sang, I heard every footstep choose its side.'
{C01} spits into the steam and watches it vanish. 'The corridor is where the city stops pretending it is one body. I have walked it enough to know the floor is only a rumor.'
{C01} nods toward the iron teeth. 'The gates do not open for titles. They open for pressure, and pressure does not forgive.'

says.text: {C01} crosses himself in the old way, then catches himself. 'You will see a throne made of gears and think the city has a heart. It has only a wheel that grinds the name into the seat.'

{C01} touches the rivet seam as if it were a bruise. 'The glass broke because the dance asked the floor to hold what the steam had already taken. I was there when the rivets went in, and the room went quiet like a mouth.'
{C01} holds out his broken hand, palm up. 'The seam took the banners first, because the banners were lighter than the truth. I held the link and felt my bones ask which way was down.'
{C01} presses his thumb to the lock. 'It is the door that keeps the dead from being rewritten. The lock is warm. It knows where it is going.'
{C01} offers the registry with both hands. 'Let me carry it. I will carry it until my hands stop being hands.'
{C01} pulls back when you reach for it. 'Pull me by the link, and the registry will only know me as a mark to strike.'
{C01} holds it against his chest. 'The registry is not paper. It is a list of who the steam will grind.'
{C01} turns the signet on his finger. 'Put it on. A hand that holds it makes the name no chain.'
{C01} does not take the black signet back. 'Do not use it like a tool. It is the last thing I was asked to keep.'
{C01} looks at the black signet. 'The black signet is black because the old wax is burned through. It still fits your finger. That is the trouble.'
{C01} grips the link nearest his shoulder. 'Hold it where I ask. I will give you my death for the hinge.'
{C01} lets the link slip from his fingers. 'Pull it, and you make me the link that breaks.'
{C01} lets the title chain rest on his forearm. 'The title chain is not heavy. It is only ever being held.'
{C01} leans close to the seam door, but does not touch it. 'The seam door is what the corridor keeps shut with its own weight. Open it, and the steam will remember the banners before you do.'
{C01} holds the engine key out, knuckles white. 'Give it to me. I will turn it once, only once.'
{C01} watches your hand without moving. 'Use the engine key without asking, and the engine will know you are a master, not a name.'
{C01} tests the engine key's weight in his palm. 'The engine key is cold until the engine has tasted it. Then it will not let go.'
{C01} braces the steam door with his broken hand. 'Stand beside me, and I can hold it open.'
{C01} leans against the steam door, breathing hard. 'Speak my name, or the steam will take it from my mouth.'
{C01} listens to the steam door. 'The steam door is not locked. It is listening.'
{C01} keeps his voice low. 'The old archive is the only room in this city that refuses to be improved. It is full of names, and the names are hungry.'
{C01} tilts his head toward the steam vent. 'The vent is where a spoken name goes when it is spoken too often. Listen, and you can hear the old city clearing its throat.'
{C01} looks down through the glass floor. 'The glass floor is beautiful the way a wound is beautiful before it closes. It will show you the chasm, and then it will choose you.'
{C01} reaches for a torn corner of the old banners, then lets it go. 'The old banners were the house before the house had a body. The seam took them, and now the steam has a voice.'
{C01} holds the struck registry page flat. 'The page is struck. I will speak the name into the steam so it is not lost.'
{C01} folds the struck registry page carefully. 'The page is struck and silent. I am only a hand that held the link.'
{C01} touches the struck registry page with one finger. 'A struck page is not clean. It is a mouth with the teeth pulled.'

C01.history: Jocelin Tanner has served the house through the descent, pressing the black signet into the heir's hand as the archive door closed and keeping the name alive in the steam. He carries the brass key to the steam doors and the chain at his wrist, believing the title is a weight that must be borne rather than a right to be worn. He has prepared for the last strike all along, so the house may survive even if it buries him.
C01.unnamed: the old servant with the chain

C02.name: Aylmer Fletcher
C02.role: the usurper steward of the engine

description.text: You see {C02} standing with the engine key in his right hand and the new registry in his left, his cuffs dry despite the steam. He bows to the hiss of the vents as if the noise were a minor fault, and says, 'The pressure requires a release.'

You see {C02} with the key hot in his right hand, the sleeve of his left arm torn where the machinery has already answered him. He still offers the registry, but his voice has gone flat, as if he is reading the machine's pressure instead of his own.

You see {C02} as the core turns and the key tugs at his wrist. He does not fight it; he only smooths the registry page. His bow is still polite, but his knuckles are white where he holds the machine's name.

You see {C02} with his left arm hanging from a strap of wet leather, the key still in his good hand. He looks at the broken joint as if it were a valve out of true. He says, 'The pressure requires a release,' without changing the shape of his voice.

You see {C02} standing whole over the crews' names, the engine key above the registry, the wet line for old ballast still shining on the page. He does not look at you; he looks at the core, and his mouth moves as if filing a report.

You see {C02}, a thin man in a steward's black coat, his gloves oiled at the fingers, the engine key on a short chain against his chest. He speaks with the calm of a man describing weather, and the steam around him keeps its distance from his cuffs.

here.text: {C02} holds the engine key against his chest and the new registry under his arm, bowing slightly to the steam as if apologizing for the noise.
{C02} holds the engine key in his good hand, his broken arm bound with wet leather, still offering the registry as if his body were a spare part.
{C02} stands over the open registry with the key raised, his face dry and his eyes on the core rather than on you.
{C02} wears his steward's coat buttoned to the throat, the engine key on a short chain, moving through the steam with small, precise bows.

says.text: 'It is not mine; it is the machine's. The pressure requires a release, and the key only keeps the release polite.'
'Yes, it is hot where the core has answered. A steward's hand is only a valve, and valves do not complain.'
'You may hold it, but do not polish it. The key remembers every hand that has tried to make it look like a title.'
'The living names are already in it. The old names are not forgotten; they are weighed, and the city is safer under the weight.'
'The ink is wet because the core has read it. Force the old registry onto this page, and you will make the machine a tomb, not a steward.'
'It is a book written by living hands. That is not cruelty; it is the difference between a city and a heap of corpses.'
'They were ballast, and the upper levels will not fall if we release what the old order is no longer.' He says it as if a pipe has been cleared.
'You are right to call it that. The old names are not ballast; they are the pressure the machine has been fed, and it will ask for more.'
'The old names were never the city. They were the weight that kept the city from becoming a hole in the earth.'
'The doors are not locked; they are let down. Steam is a cleaner death than rust, and the crews know how to hold the line.'
'The doors hold because the machine is taking its due. Ask me to open them again, and a body must be given for the opening.'
'The steam doors answer to pressure, not to titles. I only keep the pressure honest.'
'{C03} is the last witness to the old order, and witnesses make good ballast. I do not hate {C03}; I have simply given {C03} a place in the calculation.'
'Her voice is still in the steam. If you let her finish, the machine will have to choose between what it was fed and what it is being asked to keep.'
'{C03} keeps the old registry wet with her hands. That is either devotion or maintenance; the machine will not tell us which.'
'The servant's key is useful, but it is not the engine key. A name can be struck, and then the door it opened is only a hole.'
'You have made him a door. The brass key will hold the steam open, and the core will grind his name out of every page until only the turning remains.'
'{C01} follows the chain because the chain is the only thing that has ever held him. I did not break him; I only gave him a place to be broken.'
'The core is not angry. It is a pressure, and pressure does not forgive. If the upper levels are to stay out of the dark, something below must keep turning.'
'You have made it a wound. The core will still turn, but it will turn around the thing that broke it, and that thing will wear.'
'The core is the city's last honest argument. It does not care which name is on top, only that the name below is paid.'
'Your title is a seal, and seals are only useful until they are broken. I have broken it so the city would not be buried under a dead hand.'
'You have reclaimed it as a chain. The machine does not care that it is your name; it only cares that the name will keep turning.'
'The title is not a crown. It is the first gear in the machine, and it has always been turning.'
He tightens a cuff as if checking a pressure gauge. '{C05} keeps the steam crews honest. If you ask him for a reason, he will only point you at the needle.'
He traces a ring of dust on the table. 'The glass floor was a mistake, but not a cruel one. It taught the upper city where the depth began.'
He sets down a lever. 'The corridor is where the city stops pretending the earth is level. Walk it slowly, or the shadows will do the walking for you.'
He rests a palm flat on the railing. 'The gates are not doors. They are the city's last sentence, and I have been its punctuation.'

says.text: He straightens the chain at his throat. 'The gear-throne is not a chair. It is the place where the city's name is kept turning.'
He turns a valve a fraction. 'The crack was only the pressure finding its answer. The rivets were the mercy.'
{C02} taps the rim of a valve. 'The crack was a correction. The rivets were not optional. They held the glass to its rim.'
{C02} watches a shadow climb the wall. 'A seam is not a wound. It is a correction. The banners learned their weight before the people did.'
{C02} lowers his voice to the room's hum. 'The silence is not absence. It is the city being measured. Do not mistake the measurement for forgiveness.'
{C02} lays a finger on a rivet. 'The archive door is a seal, not a promise. What is kept behind it is kept by pressure, not by name.'
{C02} holds the old registry flat, as if weighing it. 'The old registry is not history. It is a list of weights. Some weights must be struck.'
{C02} closes the old registry with a bruised hand. 'The old registry is not spent. The engine only... paused.'
{C02} takes the brass key with dry fingers. 'The brass key is not for opening. It is for choosing what the engine keeps.'
{C02} holds the brass key as if it were hot. 'The brass key is not a gift. It is a wound with a handle.'
{C02} touches the chain at his throat without looking. 'The title chain is heavier than it looks. It does not hold the city down. The memory of who claimed it does.'
{C02} lays the struck page flat. 'A struck page is not a death. It is a release of pressure.'
{C02} folds the struck page carefully. 'A struck page is not a death. It is a debt the engine has not yet collected.'
{C02} points to the opening without touching it. 'The gear throat is where the city swallows its errors. Feed it cleanly, and it will not ask for more.'
{C02} leans toward the seam. 'A steam door is not a wall. It is a verdict that has not yet cooled.'
{C02} lets the steam cross his knuckles. 'The white steam is not empty. It is the old city's last breath, made useful. Breathe it, and you will learn what mercy weighs.'
{C02} taps the wall where the archive should be. 'The old archive is a reservoir of names. When the engine runs low, it will empty the reservoir into the gears.'
{C02} opens the vent a hair's width. 'The steam was only a release. You heard it in my voice; that is the point.'
{C02} leaves the vent half-open. 'The steam was not enough. Was it?'
{C02} turns the vent's wheel. 'The steam vent is not an apology. It is maintenance.'
{C02} looks down through the glass. 'The glass floor was a mistake, but a useful one. It showed the upper city that depth is not a metaphor.'
{C02} turns the black signet on his finger. 'The black signet is not a signature. It is a seal that has already been broken. Wear it, or do not pretend you are unmarked.'

C02.history: He was the steward who kept the city's pressure ledgers when the upper halls began to sink, and he learned to speak of drowned names as maintenance. He took the seat of your title because the core would not turn without a hand that would not flinch from the key. He has carried the new registry in a brass case and the engine key against his chest, waiting for the old archive to become ballast.

description.text: You see no {C03} in the lower levels; the steam only turns in the space where {C03} stood, and the archive door is sealed with no name on it.
You see {C03} as a gap in the white steam where a voice used to be. The lower levels answer with only the machine's name.
You see {C03} standing in the white steam, the registry open at {C03}'s chest, mouth moving without sound. Each name {C03} gives off the wet page rings like wet stone.
You see {C03} as a cold smear at the steam line, lips moving too slowly to hold a name. The steam has taken the last of {C03}.
You see {C03} reciting from the steam while the gear-throne stutters, each name a nail driven into the dark.
You see {C03}'s hand no longer quite a hand; the steam has pulled {C03}'s edges into the registry, and {C03} speaks through the wet paper.
You see {C03} as a drowned archivist: black gown under white steam, ink in {C03}'s hair, a registry at {C03}'s chest, speaking the old names as if they were still living.

here.text: You see {C03} with no shape left in the steam, only a cold seam in place of the archive door.
You see {C03} with the registry open at {C03}'s chest, cold hand on the steam door, speaking names into the white steam.
You see {C03} with mouth open on a name the steam has already taken, shape thinned to a wet outline.
You see {C03} with the old registry under {C03}'s arm, ink bleeding down {C03}'s sleeve, white steam curling around {C03} like a shroud.

says.text: "We are not gone. We are only... submerged." You see {C03} lift the registry, and a name rises off the wet page like breath.
"The names are not dead. The steam is only... full." The whisper breaks into the sound of water through stone.
"They drowned us to keep the engine order whole." The white steam closes over {C03}'s mouth before the last word finishes.
"Speak them, and the city will remember what it was." The voice comes from the steam, not from {C03}'s throat.
"Let me hold the door, and I will hold the names." {C03} presses a cold hand to the steam line.
"I have nothing left to give but the sound." {C03}'s mouth moves, and the sound is only water.
"One name at a time. The steam will not take all of them at once." {C03} opens the registry to the first wet page.
"Hold it where the ink is still wet." {C03} presses the old registry into your hands, its pages slick as drowned skin.
"Do not sign it with the dead." {C03}'s fingers close around yours, cold, as if the registry has already taken the signature.
"The water has read it now." {C03} touches the wet page, and the names blur like faces under water.
"The registry is not paper. It is a body." {C03} turns a page, and the steam on it moves like a pulse.
"It opens only for the dead. Speak, and let them open." The black signet fogs in your hand, and the fog takes the shape of a mouth.
"It will open for you, but not for the living." The fog on the signet spreads into a name you almost know.
"Your signet fogs because it remembers the dead." {C03}'s cold breath fogs the black metal, and the seal looks like a mouth opening.
"Let it in, and it will keep the names." {C03}'s voice thins, but the white steam holds the shape of a word.
"It has drunk too many names." The steam answers with a sound like a door sealing.
"The steam is not weather. It is a mouth." {C03} tilts {C03}'s head, and the white steam leans toward {C03}.
"{C01}. {C01}. {C01}." {C03} strikes the name into the steam, and the old seal cracks.
"The servant holds the key because the house will not let go." The whisper follows the chain at {C01}'s wrist.
"The name is a chain now." {C03} touches the wet registry, and the ink under {C01}'s name has gone black.
"{C01} is a link, not a man." The voice is flat, as if the name has already been filed away.
"{C02} has written the old names as ballast." The registry under {C03}'s hand is already steaming.
"Behind {C02}, the dead are naming {C02}." The whisper comes from the steam, not from {C03}.
"{C02} calls the drowning a release." {C03}'s mouth moves, but the steam carries the word away.
"Sealed. Sealed. Sealed." The voice is gone, leaving only the sound of the door closing.
"The machine has taken its name." The white steam behind {C03} is empty of recitation.
"The archive is not a room. It is a throat." {C03} presses a palm to the steam door, and the door answers with a low grind.
A rivet of sound falls from {C03}. "{C05} signs the crew ledger with a hot rivet. {C05} is not evil; {C05} is only the hand the machine uses to keep the dead out of the air."
The whisper becomes a thin bell. "The glass was polished to make the dead look like dancers below. Now it only shows what the living will not carry down."
The whisper moves sideways through {C03}. 'In the transition corridor the floor forgets down. The banners remember out. What drops is filed.'
A cold mineral breath moves under the whisper. 'The engine gates do not ask who enters. They ask what is left in the seal. The old names are the seal.'

says.text: Water in stone widens under the voice. 'The gear-throne engine room is the city's throat. It swallows the old names and turns them into heat, so the throne keeps its iron crown.'
A wet crack runs through the whisper. 'The cracked ballroom was not a break. It was a sentence. The glass opened over the steam, and the rivets closed the archive before the first name was spoken.'

Something in the voice falls upward. 'The gravity seam is the earth learning a new word. It pulls the banners down like a tongue learning taste. The first it swallowed was the banner of the drowned court.'
A silence gathers in the whisper. 'The last name is not a name. It is the silence before the gear-throne remembers its teeth. When it speaks, the city is a wound with a schedule.'
A cold finger presses the air. 'The archive door was sealed with rivets. A door that remembers is a hinge the living cannot bear. Unmake the seal, and it is answering, not opening.'
The whisper thins. 'The archive door is not locked. It is only waiting to be told that the dead are no longer permitted to be remembered. The rivets are not the lock. They are the proof.'
The wet air is held as if it were a page. 'The old registry is still wet, and it still speaks. Hold it where the steam cannot read it, and it answers with your name.'
The voice is spent. 'The old registry is a corpse with ink still moving. Do not let them call it a record. It is a wound that remembers you.'
The whisper sharpens. 'The black signet opens only for the dead. It is not a key. It is a promise that the dead will be allowed to open the living.'
A cold ring of sound passes under the voice. 'The black signet has learned to bite. It does not open for the dead now. It opens for the thing that has eaten the dead.'
A chain of droplets hangs from the words. 'The title chain is a collar of offices, not a crown. It does not make you noble. It makes you a name the city can hang its weight on.'
The voice slides into a wall. 'The seam door is where the corridor stops being a corridor and becomes a list. Cross it, and you are filed under whatever the steam decides you were.'
The whisper turns like a lock. 'The engine key is not a key. It is a lock that has learned to turn itself. Put it in your hand, and it asks your name to be used as a tooth.'
A chewing sound moves under the voice. 'The gear throat is the part of the machine that swallows names before they can become prayers. When it chews, the old order is ground into fuel.'
The voice becomes a slow, heavy turn. 'The gear-throne is not a seat. It is a verdict. It sits where the city's old heart was, and it crowns whatever can be turned.'
The steam holds the voice. 'The steam door is the archive's mouth when the archive is afraid. Let it hold you, and it keeps your name in the cold. Let it open, and it spends you.'
The steam takes half the sentence. 'The steam door has forgotten the shape of the archive. It only opens for what is already being erased.'
The whisper stays clear in the white. 'The white steam is not heat. It is forgetting made visible. It does not erase. It edits, and it edits in the plural.'
The white steam eats the end of the voice. 'The white steam is the clerk. It has taken the old registry, and now it writes you out in a hand you will not recognize.'
The voice becomes a room. 'The old archive is the last place where the city still knows it has a past. Keep it sealed, and it remains a name no one can be forced to speak.'
The voice is a wet ruin. 'The old archive is not a building. It is a throat full of names, and they have poured the engine's order down it. What remains is only the taste.'
A thin hiss comes from the voice. 'The steam vent is the city's breath when it is dreaming of being open. Put your ear to it, and you hear the names they are trying to forget, spelled backwards.'

C03.history: Matilda Scrope was the archivist of the old house, keeper of the names that kept the city's title alive. When the first steam tides rose, she walked into the white line with the registry and did not come back, and the drowned city has been speaking her since. She recites the old names in the present tense because, in the lower levels, the death of the old order has not yet been allowed to finish.

description.text: {C05} gives {C02}'s key a half-nod before he looks at you, his hand open on the lever as if the engine's order still has weight. When the core lurches, he checks the key's heat before he checks the men.
{C05} does not look at {C02}'s key. His fingers work the bleed valve with the patience of a man who has learned that steam keeps its own ledger. The core answers, and his jaw stays tight.
When {C01}'s name comes near, {C05} checks the door chain first, as if loyalty were a pressure reading he can trust. 'The crew holds,' he says, almost proud.
{C05} watches {C01}'s broken hand and keeps his own grip on the core, as if the crew's names were safer than any man's. He does not say pity. He tightens the valve.
{C03}'s dead names make {C05} still. He wipes his mouth with the back of his hand before he answers. He listens to the steam like a man counting a debt.
{C05} lets {C03}'s voice pass into the steam without turning, as if the lower levels had already been answered. His eyes stay on the core, not the door.
{C05}'s men stand too still behind him, eyes on your hands, and he does not tell them to look away. The new registry lies open on his shoulder. His hands are black with the core's oil.

{C05} braces against the core, shoulders straining, face grey with the effort of keeping the lower levels from falling. His lever hand does not let go, even as the steam begins to take the sound from his voice.

{C05} is a heavy man in a boiled-leather apron, cuffs black with scale, a brass gauge strapped to his belt. He speaks like a man counting what the machine takes, and he does not waste breath on comfort.

here.text: {C05} stands with his back to the gear-throne, keeping the core's wheel from swinging, as if {C02}'s engine key still counts.
{C05} keeps his eyes on the core more than the key, thumb on the bleed valve, ready to let the steam decide.
{C05} checks the door chain before he looks at you, his grip on the lever steady as if {C01}'s loyalty were a pressure reading.
{C05} watches {C01}'s broken hand and keeps his own grip on the core, as if the crew's names were safer than any man's.
{C05} listens to the steam with his eyes closed, waiting for {C03}'s dead names to finish before he speaks.
{C05} keeps his face turned from the steam, thumb on the bleed valve, as if {C03}'s voice were already answered.

says.text: '{C02}'s key is a fair key. It opens what it is keyed for.' He keeps his hand on the bleed.
'The key is hot, and hot keys burn the hand that trusts them.' He does not look at {C02}.
'{C01}'s name is on the door chain. The crew holds.' He almost sounds proud.
'{C01}'s hand is broken, but a broken hand still opens doors; that is all the loyalty the core asks.' He says it low.
'{C03}'s dead names are in the steam; I have heard them counted.' He wipes oil from his eyes.
'{C03}'s voice is gone into the white, and the lower levels do not keep what is spoken there.' He does not look at the steam.
'The core does not argue; it turns, or it takes.' He pats the valve stem without looking.
'Under {C02}'s order, the crew keeps its names.' He checks the hooks.
'{C02}'s order breaks, and the crew is only steam with a payroll.' He says it low.
'{C01} holds the door because he chose to.' He almost sounds proud.
'{C01} holds the door because the chain will not let go.' He does not say it with pity.
'{C03}'s dead names are on their lips before they can stop it.' He wipes oil from his eyes.
'{C03}'s dead names are in the steam now, and the crew does not answer them.' He looks at the core.
'They are not my men; the core made them.' He glances at the crew, and they do not blink.

says.text: '{C02}'s key makes it a registry, not a wound.' He almost believes it.
'{C02}'s key has not mended it; it has only made the wound official.' He does not look at the key.
'{C01}'s hand held the door, and your hands held the seal.' He sounds as if he is comparing debts.
'{C01}'s hand is broken, and your seal is broken; the core prefers that.' He does not smile.
'{C03} whispered the names, and the seal opened for them.' He looks at the steam.
'{C03}'s voice is in the steam, and the seal is in your hands; one of them is going to be fed.' He says it low.
'Look at your own hands; the old order's last seal is already broken, and you carried it in.' He points at your palms.
'{C02}'s conviction is clean; I have seen the registry.' He gives a short nod.
'{C02}'s conviction is a bruise, and the engine will press it again.' He says it low.
'{C01}'s hand is on his door, and {C02}'s key is in the lock.' He almost sounds proud.
He does not smile. “{C01}’s hand is on {C02}’s door, and {C02}’s key is in the lock; neither of them is safe.”
He says it like a pressure warning. “{C03}’s names are behind his key.”
He does not look at {C02}. “{C03}’s names are behind his key, and the steam has already swallowed them.”
He does not look at {C02}. “{C02} has the key, and the key has the engine.”
He checks a valve, not out of respect. “{C01}’s loyalty holds. He’s the only promise in this city I’d bet a valve on.”
He spits into the steam. “{C01}’s loyalty is gone. He’s a dead man walking in good clothes. I’ll send a man to make it quick.”
He turns a wrench slowly. “{C01}’s an old man with a servant’s patience. I’ve seen him hold a door against steam that would peel paint.”
He taps a wet pipe. “{C03}’s memory is still in the steam. It’s not a ghost. It’s a debt with a name.”
He looks at the waterline. “{C03}’s memory is drowned. The old city’s last witness is just water now. Ask the tide, not me.”
He wipes his hands on his apron. “{C03} was an archivist, which means she kept the city’s sins in a ledger. The water keeps them better.”
He picks at a rusted rivet. “The glass-floored ballroom is a beautiful lie with a floor. Look down too long and you’ll learn what the aristocrats are hiding under their feet.”
He nods toward the dark. “The transition corridor is where the city stops being a map. Walk it like you’re already dead and the floor is a suggestion.”
He rests a palm on the gate. “The engine gates don’t care about your title. They care about your torque.”

says.text: He listens to the gears. “The gear-throne engine room is where the city tells the truth about its own weight. Stand in it long enough and you stop asking for permission.”
He counts rivets with one eye. “When the ballroom cracked, my crews riveted the archive door shut. A door’s a promise, and the steam don’t keep promises.”
He points at the ceiling. “A gravity seam is the city’s spine slipping. We lost a banner, but a banner’s a warning, not a loss.”
He goes quiet as the gears slow. “The last name is the silence between the gears. When it speaks, the city learns what it was before it was a machine.”
He holds the book’s edge, not the page. “The old registry is where the city keeps its grudges. I’ve seen a name in it hold a man’s family hostage longer than a chain.”
He turns the brass key between his fingers. “The brass key opens the old registry, not the core. It’s a pretty little coffin for a name.”
He watches the key’s teeth. “{C02} has the conviction to stand whole with that key. That makes him either the city’s savior or its fuse.”
He grips the lever. “{C02}’s conviction is cracked, and the engine key is a live wire in a wet man’s fist. I’ve seen worse ends; I’ve seen fewer.”
He doesn’t touch the engine key. “The engine key is the only object in this city that knows what it’s worth. It doesn’t fit in a hand; it fits in a choice.”
He rolls the wheel’s edge with a greased thumb. “The seal wheel is the city’s way of saying yes with a scar. Turn it, and something older than your title turns back.”
He signs nothing. “The new registry is a fresh page for the same debt. Men sign it with their hands, and later the engine collects.”
He kicks a bolt. “The lower doors are the city’s teeth. When they open, they don’t ask if you’re invited.”
He points to the throne’s axle. “{C02} stands whole at the gear-throne. The engine order stands whole. I’ll put my men on the hooks and let the math run.”
He checks a hook. “{C02} is broken before the gear-throne. The throne will eat him and call it ceremony.”
He keeps his hands on the railing. “The gear-throne doesn’t crown anyone. It selects a load.”
He holds a key to the lock. “A lock’s a question. The registry lock asks if you’re still who the page says you are.”
He leans into the hiss. “The steam door’s the only door in the city that tells the truth about what’s on the other side: hot, wet, and expensive.”
He breathes slow. “White steam is the only witness down here. It gets in your lungs and keeps what it sees.”
He tests a hook. “The core hooks are the lower levels’ last argument against falling. I’ve put men on them; I’ve counted the men it left behind.”
He rests his forearm on the lever. “The engine lever is a promise with a handle. Pull it, and the city pays in weight.”
